Body and hair: athletic build; a shaggy layered wolf cut with side-swept bangs; ripe wheat-gold hair scattered with tiny bright spark-white glints like struck flint.
Hair: her hair is worn exactly as described above — loose, long or cut as named; do not pin it up into a bun or tuck it under goggles or a hat unless the hair above is an updo.
Expression: a small closed-lip smile that reaches the eyes.
Her element, carried in her design: cerium: a soft, silvery-grey rare-earth metal, the most abundant of the rare earths, named in 1803 for the newly found small world Ceres, goddess of grain and harvest; its shavings catch fire in air when scratched, and alloyed with iron into ferrocerium it becomes the flint of lighters and fire-starters, throwing showers of hot yellow-white sparks when struck; pale cerium oxide powder polishes glass and lenses crystal clear.
Anatomy: one head, two arms and two legs, each joined at its natural joint; natural hands with five fingers.

Costume: late-Victorian industrial dress — a high-necked blouse with a waistcoat or a tailored tail coat, leather gloves, a work apron or utility belt with brass fittings, goggles hung at the neck or a small instrument as ornament; below, a short bustle skirt and laced boots; the traits above as colour accents. No crown unless the opening line says she wears one; steam, pipes and gauges in the scene.
Silhouette: a heavy leather work apron with rolled sleeves, a tool harness and one big gauntlet glove — a hands-on engineer's shape. Only the overall shape is fixed; design the details freely in the element's materials and palette. This silhouette overrides the overall shape of the costume above.
Colours: ripe wheat gold, flint grey, hot spark yellow-white, pale ceria cream.
Exposure (bold): her outfit opens to show skin — the neckline opened down to the sternum with natural cleavage, bare forearms, and bare legs above the boots or through a high slit where the silhouette allows; pieces stay symmetrical. Nothing slipped off. Intimate areas covered; no corset; keep the costume above, material and palette.

4. SCENE
World: around 1903, an alpine works in Carinthia where a new iron-cerium alloy is cast into slim flint rods: a casting floor of glowing rod moulds, display trays of brass pocket lighters and gas lighters, a test bench where each flint is struck with a steel file and showers bright yellow sparks.
Pose: standing confidently, her body turned slightly while her face looks toward the viewer.
Light: bright warm sunlight with soft sky light bounced from white clouds.
Composition: vertical 2:3 full-body framing with modest headroom and clear space below the boots — the whole figure from the top of her head or headpiece to both feet stays inside the frame, occupying about four-fifths of the image height, with the same camera distance in every world; her hands stay inside the frame. Camera level with her face with natural portrait perspective; her head level, chin neither raised nor tucked — no upward perspective on her face, no wide-angle distortion, no low angle, no close crop.

5. CONSTRAINTS
One figure only; no text or numbers except her element's own chemical symbol (Ce) and atomic number (58) — and those only as part of the scene: engraved, embroidered or glowing on her costume, a banner, a sign or a machine, never as a floating label, corner badge, periodic-table tile, caption or overlay on the picture; no logo or watermark.
